newsitem.title: USA: FDA request for tobacco regs no surprise - analysts.
newsitem.headline: FDA request for tobacco regs no surprise - analysts.

text.p: A request by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration that a federal judge permit regulation of the U.S. tobacco industry was not at all surprising, industry analysts said on Monday.
But Wall Street would watch for clues on the future of legal wrangles surrounding smoking, after the recent resignation of FDA Commissioner David Kessler, analysts said.

"The interesting thing now, with the Kessler resignation, is whether there is an impetus to resolve the tobacco regulation issue via negotiation instead of the courtroom," said David Adelman, a tobacco analyst at Dean Witter Reynolds.

A FDA request on Monday that a federal court turn down a tobacco industry request to block tough new tobacco regulations, was a response to a brief filed on October 15 by the tobacco industry, analysts said.

The agency said in a court filing its sharp restrictions on tobacco billboards, vending machines and sports advertisements were consistent with the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act. The tobacco industry contends the FDA does not have the right to regulate tobacco products.
"This is exactly what you'd expect," Schroeder Wertheim & Co tobacco analyst Robert Cummins said.
On October 15, cigarette makers and advertisers filed a motion in the U.S. District Court for central North Carolina for a summary judgement against the FDA.

The motion argued that the U.S. Congress never authorized the FDA to regulate cigarettes and smokeless tobacco and that the act did not authorize the FDA to regulate these products as "drugs" or medical devices.
"The FDA had until December 2 to file a response," Cummins said, adding that this was part of normal legal procedure.
Industry giant Philip Morris Cos Inc took the news in stride, closing up 1/8 at 103-1/4.
The next move would come from the tobacco industry, which had until December 23 to reply to the FDA, analysts said.
The hearing, before U.S. District Judge William Osteen, was set for February 10 in the middle district of North Carolina, analysts said.
In the meantime, some analysts said attention would focus on the internal workings of the FDA.
"Wall Street might try to look through the filings for hints about the Kessler resignation," Gary Black, an analyst at Sanford Bernstein & Co, said.
Kessler, who is vocally anti-smoking, will leave his post as chief of the FDA in early 1997 after a successor is named, FDA officials said.
Dean Witter's Adelman said Kessler's resignation might make it easier for the Clinton administration to change its stance on tobacco regulation.
Others were more sceptical. "Kessler is still there, and it is still his move for the near-term," Cummins said.
"In the future, depending on Kessler's successor, and the administration's tendency to bend with the wind, the issue of regulating the tobacco industry could fall out of the spotlight," he said.
